title: What is busy-waiting or spinning, what is a spin lock, what does Thread.onSpinWait() do, and when does spinning help versus harm?

s1_definition.profdef: Busy-waiting (spinning) is when a thread repeatedly checks a condition in a tight loop instead of blocking and yielding the CPU. A spin lock is a lock implemented by spinning on an atomic flag using compare-and-swap until it is acquired, rather than parking the thread. Spinning avoids the cost of suspending and resuming a thread (a context switch, typically on the order of microseconds), so it wins when the wait is expected to be extremely short and a CPU core is available to spin. It harms when the wait is long or cores are oversubscribed, because the spinning thread burns CPU doing nothing and starves other work. `Thread.onSpinWait()`, added in Java 9, is a hint to the CPU that the current loop is a spin-wait, letting the processor optimize power and pipeline behavior (for example x86 emits the PAUSE instruction) and improving the performance of the sibling thread.
s1_definition.analogy: A spinning teller is one who, instead of going on break while waiting for the vault door to unlock, stands right at the door repeatedly jiggling the handle every microsecond. If the door is about to open in a blink, this is faster than walking to the break room and being paged back (a context switch). But if the door will be locked for ten minutes, the teller is wasting energy and blocking the corridor while accomplishing nothing — far better to go on break (block). `Thread.onSpinWait` is the teller tapping the handle gently instead of yanking it hard, which tells the building (CPU) "I am just waiting, conserve power and let my colleague work faster."
s1_definition.oneliner: Spinning trades CPU cycles to avoid a context switch, so it helps only for very short waits on an available core; use Thread.onSpinWait to hint the CPU, and block instead when the wait is long or cores are scarce.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Busy-waiting (spinning) is when a thread repeatedly checks a condition in a tight loop instead of blocking and yielding the CPU. A spin lock is a lock implemented by spinning on an atomic flag using compare-and-swap until it is acquired, rather than parking the thread. Spinning avoids the cost of suspending and resuming a thread (a context switch, typically on the order of microseconds), so it wins when the wait is expected to be extremely short and a CPU core is available to spin. It harms when the wait is long or cores are oversubscribed, because the spinning thread burns CPU doing nothing and starves other work. `Thread.onSpinWait()`, added in Java 9, is a hint to the CPU that the current loop is a spin-wait, letting the processor optimize power and pipeline behavior (for example x86 emits the PAUSE instruction) and improving the performance of the sibling thread.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A spinning teller is one who, instead of going on break while waiting for the vault door to unlock, stands right at the door repeatedly jiggling the handle every microsecond. If the door is about to open in a blink, this is faster than walking to the break room and being paged back (a context switch). But if the door will be locked for ten minutes, the teller is wasting energy and blocking the corridor while accomplishing nothing — far better to go on break (block). `Thread.onSpinWait` is the teller tapping the handle gently instead of yanking it hard, which tells the building (CPU) "I am just waiting, conserve power and let my colleague work faster."

**One line to remember:** Spinning trades CPU cycles to avoid a context switch, so it helps only for very short waits on an available core; use Thread.onSpinWait to hint the CPU, and block instead when the wait is long or cores are scarce.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an ultra-low-latency trade sequencer that assigns a strictly increasing sequence number to each incoming order. The critical section is just a few instructions, held for well under a microsecond, and the machine has spare cores. Here, a thread that parks and is woken for every order would add context-switch latency that dwarfs the work. This is exactly where a spin lock with Thread.onSpinWait wins: the waiting thread spins for the blink it takes the holder to release, acquiring the lock with minimal latency.

Problem 2 — The same pattern applied to a slow operation, like a sequencer that does disk I/O inside the critical section, would be a disaster: waiting threads would spin for milliseconds, pinning cores at 100 percent for nothing. The code contrasts the correct short-critical-section spin against why you must never spin on a long wait, and shows bounded spinning that falls back to parking.

The code builds a `SpinLock` using AtomicBoolean and onSpinWait, a `TradeSequencer` guarded by it that hands out sequence numbers to orders for RELIANCE, and a demo with multiple threads acquiring sequence numbers concurrently, plus a bounded-spin variant that parks after a spin budget.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a TradeSequencer guarded by a SpinLock, four threads each requesting five sequence numbers for RELIANCE, twenty total.

Step 1: Thread A calls `next`, which calls `lock.lock()`. The AtomicBoolean is false, so the CAS succeeds immediately (false to true) and A owns the lock without spinning.

Step 2: While A holds the lock for the single `++sequence` operation, thread B calls `lock.lock()`. Its CAS fails because the flag is true, so B enters the spin loop, calling `Thread.onSpinWait()` each iteration. On x86 this emits PAUSE, conserving power and letting a sibling thread run faster. B is burning its core, but only for the handful of nanoseconds A needs.

Step 3: Thread A finishes the increment (sequence becomes 1) and calls `unlock()`, setting the flag back to false.

Step 4: Thread B's next CAS attempt succeeds, so B acquires the lock, increments sequence to 2, and releases. Threads C and D proceed the same way. Because the critical section is a single instruction, the spin time is minuscule and no context switch ever happened.

Step 5: Across all four threads and twenty requests, every sequence number is unique and strictly increasing with no gaps and no duplicates, proving the spin lock enforced mutual exclusion. The output reports twenty unique numbers and a max of twenty.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: assigned 20 unique sequence numbers (expected 20)
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: max sequence = 20
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  4 threads request sequence numbers for RELIANCE (tiny critical section)
    │
    ▼
  SpinLock (AtomicBoolean locked)
    │
    ├─ Thread A: CAS false→true ── owns lock
    │     ++sequence = 1 ── unlock (set false)
    │
    ├─ Thread B: CAS fails (true) ── SPIN:
    │     while(!CAS) Thread.onSpinWait()   ← PAUSE, few ns only
    │     CAS succeeds → ++sequence = 2 ── unlock
    │
    ├─ Thread C/D: same tiny spin-then-acquire
    ▼
  20 unique, strictly increasing sequence numbers, NO context switch

  ─ WHEN SPINNING HARMS (contrast) ─
  long critical section (disk I/O) → waiters spin for ms → cores at 100% idle work
  oversubscribed cores → spinner blocks the holder → use bounded spin + park
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Busy-waiting, or spinning, is when a thread checks a condition in a tight loop instead of blocking and giving up the CPU. A spin lock is the simplest form of this: an atomic flag that a thread flips from free to held using compare-and-swap in a loop, retrying immediately on failure rather than going to sleep. The whole point is to avoid the cost of suspending and resuming a thread, because a context switch costs on the order of microseconds, and if the wait is shorter than that, spinning is the faster choice.

Thread.onSpinWait, which arrived in Java 9, is a hint I put inside any spin loop. It does not change the logic at all; it tells the processor that this loop is a spin-wait, so on x86 it emits the PAUSE instruction, which conserves power during the spin, avoids a memory-ordering penalty when the loop exits, and lets a sibling hyperthread on the same core run faster. It is essentially free and I always include it when I deliberately spin.

The judgement call is when spinning helps versus harms. It helps when three conditions hold: the expected wait is very short, shorter than a context switch; there is a spare core so the spinner does not steal time from the thread that will release the lock; and contention is low. The textbook case is a lock protecting just a few instructions. Spinning harms when the wait is long, because then the thread pins a whole core doing nothing, and it is especially dangerous when cores are oversubscribed, because the spinner can end up scheduled on the same core as the lock holder and actually prevent the holder from running to release the lock. So spinning is a latency optimization, not a throughput optimization; it shaves microseconds at the cost of CPU. The pragmatic answer in between is bounded or adaptive spinning: spin a limited number of times, then fall back to parking the thread, which is exactly what the JVM's own locks do, and the reason I almost never hand-write a spin lock in application code and instead use ReentrantLock or synchronized.

At National Bank of India the one place I used an explicit spin lock was the trade sequencer, which assigns a strictly increasing sequence number to every incoming order. The critical section was a single increment, held for well under a microsecond, and the box had spare cores, so a thread that parked and woke for every order would have added latency that dwarfed the work. A spin lock with onSpinWait acquired the lock in the blink it took the holder to release, with no context switch. But I was very clear that the same pattern around anything slow, like disk I/O in the critical section, would be a catastrophe. The sentence I give interviewers is that spinning trades CPU cycles to dodge a context switch, so it only pays off for provably tiny waits on an available core, I always add Thread.onSpinWait to the loop, and the moment the wait could be long or cores are scarce, I block instead or use bounded spinning that parks.
